AlternateTargets: Attend to the root, and the Way emerges as it takes hold
SearchAliases: work at the root way grows
Senses.Note: The classical saying means that a cultivated person works at the root; once the root is established, the Way grows. Tian’an uses it to ask what the root of ritual is after setting Chan exchanges beside Confucian lines; Baichi raises a staff and asks his listeners what the root is; Yushan warns that claiming to have found a root without its living effects still misses the point; Pu’an identifies the root with what is already present before words; Wu’an reads it as a close analogy for the original face. The same sentence serves five distinct Chan inquiries into what “root” can mean.

Senses.Explanation: “The cultivated person works at the root; when the root stands, the Way grows” joins the work of grounding to what arises from it. Senses.PreferredTarget: A person of principle may value wealth, but acquires it by the right way
SearchAliases: a person of principle may value wealth, but acquires it by the right way
Senses.Note: “A person of principle may value wealth, but acquires it by the right way” enters Chan records in more than one turn. Yunwai asks why Dongshan Xiaocong’s use of the proverb should count as a particular lineage’s speech. Zixian lifts his staff, refuses Bajiao’s giving and taking, then voices the line himself. Huizhou revisits Dongshan’s answer and proposes his own. Yushan uses the proverb to ask why a treasure-holding figure cannot release its ingot. Wealth becomes an image for grasping, exchange, and the limits of an answer.

Senses.PreferredTarget: Who would dare put a price on the sovereign’s treasure?
AlternateTargets: The king’s treasure: who could presume to name its value?
SearchAliases: who dares price the king treasure
Senses.Note: Later Tang Emperor Zhuangzong tells Xinghua that he has won a treasure in the Central Plain but no one can price it. Asked to show it, he spreads the bands of his court headwear, and Xinghua answers with this question. The line can honor the emperor’s display, yet later masters disagree about whether Xinghua truly met him: Baichi praises both, Yingshan asks who recognizes the treasure, Lianyue amplifies its worth, Hongzhi writes verses on it, and Minshu would answer differently. Its value lies in the encounter, not a market price for an object.

Senses.Explanation: In Caodong technical discourse, lord and minister name a relational configuration used to explain upright and inclined positions and their interaction. Caoshan Benji maps lord to the upright position and minister to the inclined, then names minister-facing-lord, lord-regarding-minister, and lord-and-minister accord. A later Caoshan quotation repeats that mapping. Juelang Daosheng equates arriving within both with lord and minister according. Yinqian identifies the Caodong house through their accord. Langting Ting disputes the later classification of Caoshan's answers as five lord-and-minister positions. Shixi Xinyue sets the five positions beside Linji's three mysteries and three essentials. Shaoyuan says the five positions are all penetrated when host and guest accord. These uses establish a technical relational family while preserving disagreement about its historical systematization.

Senses.Explanation: The rotted axe handle is the records’ time-lapse allusion: a woodcutter watches an immortal chess game and returns after his handle has decayed. The Chan corpus does not usually retell that background in full; it repeatedly names its visible pieces. Fang'an Xian says that when the game ends no one knows where to go, leaving “the Lanke man” sorrowful in the empty mountain (局罷不知何處去空山惆悵爛柯人). Yuan'an Feng repeats, “the Lanke woodcutter doubts there is a road” (爛柯樵子疑無路). Yongjue Yuanxian lists taking up “the Lanke axe” beside propping a broken-legged pot, while Zhongfeng Mingben says the axe handle has rotted and vanished but the game is not yet finished. Wansong Xingxiu explicitly says that an earlier verse already has the original account of the Lanke woodcutter (已有爛柯樵子本傳). The Zen-specific bend is this repeated use of the rotted handle, woodcutter, unfinished game, and lost road as a compact allusion in case verse and formal speech. The outside story remains an inherited historical lead except where the Chan text names these elements directly.

Senses.Explanation: “Fry in oil over a fierce fire” is Muzhou Daoming’s compact answer when a monk asks, “What is Chan?” The wording preserves an extreme cooking image, and Muzhou supplies no prose gloss for it. Wuyi Yuanlai later quotes the inherited answer among cases he explicitly calls “without semantic flavor.” Yongjue Yuanxian raises the same old answer, appraises the inherited cluster, and contrasts it with answers of his own. Feiyin Tongrong also speaks the image directly at the close of his own hall address, providing an independent use outside Muzhou’s question-and-answer. Wuyi and Yongjue actively comment on one inherited Muzhou case rather than supplying separate ancient speakers; none of these records makes this one image a universal or literal definition of Chan.

Senses.Explanation: A fierce tiger does not eat meat that submits before it pictures the tiger declining prey already lying prostrate. Gulin Qingmao pairs the line with a fine hawk that does not strike a dead rabbit. Tian'an Sheng repeats the pair, then says that if the listener brings a Linji shout he will block the listener's throat, and if the listener brings a Deshan staff he will break it in two. When a monk tells Liangting Jingting, 'I knew it,' Liangting gives the tiger line; the monk then shouts, and Liangting calls the shout excessive. Zuliang Chaoqi calls for anyone willing to risk his life before Xuansha's released tiger; when nobody comes forward, he gives the line and leaves. Xiaoyan Debao raises Yunmen Wenyan's encounter with an approaching monk, criticizes Yunmen's handling, and places the phrase in his own counterfactual response. The retained lamp recension preserves Jingqing Daofu giving the saying after the monk says that he has failed or disappointed Jingqing. These passages repeatedly place prostrate or already-yielding prey beside a response, challenge, or exchange that has stopped short.

Senses.Explanation: An intimate pillow-and-tears image serves as a paradoxical closing response to rival Chan positions, case comments and questions about life and death. Three further recorded uses spell the full couplet with 兩行淚, a same-job wording variant of 雙行淚. In a Buddha-birthday hall sermon Yongjue Yuanxian compares Yunmen's striking reply with other elders' answers and says their rivalry still yields only one fragment. Asked what he himself would say, he closes with the two-sided tears on a lovers' pillow. The image is his present answer, not a report of an actual grieving couple. In a separate question session a monk asks Yongjue Yuanxian about the point of Bodhidharma coming west. Yongjue calls it 'stirring waves without wind'; when the monk asks what follows, he directly gives the pillow-and-tears couplet. This is a second local answer by the same teacher, distinct from his birthday sermon. Suru Honghan raises Wansong's teaching on the Caodong handling of two edges. He credits it with illuminating the tradition but asks whether it still invites criticism, then voices the pillow-and-tears couplet before adding his own verse. The selected line is his current case appraisal. Weilin Daopei warns his audience not to treat life and death as casual words. After comparing real treasure with a worthless shard, he asks whether an old no-mind saying is gold or rubble and closes with the pillow-and-tears couplet. The line is his present challenge in this address. At his temple installation Shanhui Huan considers whether his presence in the Buddha hall sounds like praise or blame. He closes that question with two rows of tears on the mandarin-duck pillow, half love and half resentment. The couplet is his current answer in the hall, not a report of an actual bereaved couple. A monk asks Wenmu Nian why a good teacher calls Buddha and patriarchs names. He replies directly with the paired tears of longing and resentment on a lovers' pillow. The image is his answer to the apparent contradiction, and another monk immediately repeats the question and receives a different reply. Senses.Explanation: A finished embroidery can be shown; the needle that produced it is not handed over. Chan speakers use the image to distinguish demonstration from a formula another person can simply receive. Feiyin closes a hall address on how to teach by displaying the saying; Liaoan couples it with a staff gesture when asked where the way comes from. Baichi turns the difference into a live interview about the staff, embroidered pattern, and needle. Miyun ends a discourse on everyday activity with the saying rather than a rule for realizing the true body.

Senses.PreferredTarget: You may look at the embroidered mandarin ducks, but I do not pass the gold needle to anyone
AlternateTargets: The embroidered ducks are yours to see; the gold needle is not handed on
SearchAliases: show embroidery do not pass needle
Senses.Note: The finished embroidery can be seen, but the gold needle that made it is not handed over. In Chan exchanges, a teacher may offer a visible answer or demonstration while declining to make its source a thing another person can simply receive. Tian'an speaks it while holding a needle; others use it after a gesture, a question, or a sermon. The image can be a challenge to find one's own way, rather than a claim that the teacher guards a secret tool.
